beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Adwait Changan, and this video is about when you should not build an AI agent. Today we are going to learn a three-part test, and then watch most ordinary tasks fail it. That is not a pessimistic framing. It is the most useful thing anyone can tell you before you start.

show.event: composer on cream; the fellow names himself and the topic

props.segment: When Not to Build an Agent
props.command: Before I build this as an agent — should it be one at all?
output: Three conditions, and all of them have to hold.
Scored against six ordinary tasks, two pass.
Knowing which condition fails tells you what to build instead.

beats.narration_text: The test is three questions. Does the task need something done, rather than described. Is a wrong step cheap to undo. And can you tell success from failure without reading every step yourself. All three, not two.

layers.title: Doing, not describing
layers.sub: there is a real action at the end of it

layers.title: Cheap to undo
layers.sub: a wrong step costs minutes, not money or trust

layers.title: Checkable
layers.sub: success is distinguishable from failure without reading every step

props.caption: Two out of three is the most dangerous score there is.

beats.narration_text: Which is one line of code and deliberately unforgiving. Three booleans joined by and. No weighting, no score out of ten, no mostly. A task that fails one condition fails the test, because the whole point is to stop you averaging away the condition that will hurt.

show.event: the absence of any weighting holds

props.title: decide.py — verdict()

beats.narration_text: So I scored six tasks people genuinely hand to agents. Not strawmen. The things in every tutorial and every internal pitch deck. Two of the six pass. The interesting part is not the count. It is which condition each failure trips on.

props.title: Six Ordinary Tasks
props.body: The things in every tutorial and every internal pitch deck. Two of six pass. What matters is which condition each failure trips on.

beats.narration_text: Reformatting files passes. Fixing failing tests passes. Drafting a reply fails on doing, because it produces text for you to send. Triaging tickets fails on two. Research fails on checkable. And emailing the quarterly numbers fails on undo, which is the one that ends careers.

show.event: the two passing tasks write on
drafting and triage land with their gaps
the quarterly email lands last, failing on undo

props.artifactHeading: Two pass. The rest name their own gap.
artifactLines: Reformat a folder of CSVs              AGENT    -
Draft a reply for me to send           NOT YET  doing
Triage and close support tickets       NOT YET  undoable, checkable
Research and summarise a topic         NOT YET  doing, checkable
Run the test suite and fix failures    AGENT    -
Email the quarterly numbers to board   NOT YET  undoable

beats.narration_text: And a failed condition is not a rejection. It is an instruction. Fails on doing? Build a drafting tool, not an agent. Fails on undo? Put a confirmation in front of the irreversible step. Fails on checkable? That one is the real work, and it comes before the agent, not after.

show.event: 'Which one failed?' appears at the source
the three remedies light in order

feeds.label: doing — build a drafting tool instead
undo — add confirmation before the irreversible step

props.destTitle: the task may pass once the gap is closed
props.arcCaption: the test tells you what to build, not just whether to

beats.narration_text: Now the result that argues against my own rubric. Each condition fails exactly twice across these six tasks. There is no single villain, no one thing you can fix and be done. If I had found that checkable failed five times, this test would be mostly about checkability and I would have said so.

show.event: checkable lands at 2 of 6, in terracotta

props.artifactHeading: No single villain, which is itself the finding

beats.narration_text: Two out of three is the score that gets people hurt, and the combination matters. Doing and undoable without checkable is an agent that acts confidently and nobody notices when it is wrong. Doing and checkable without undo is one where you find out afterwards and cannot take it back.

show.event: all three lands last in terracotta

props.sparkLine: Two of three is the trap.
items: Doing + undo, not checkable — acts wrong, unnoticed
Doing + checkable, no undo — you find out too late
Undo + checkable, not doing — you built a tool, call it one
props.caption: The first two feel like success while you are building them.

beats.narration_text: And the honest reason this matters is cost. An agent is not a free upgrade over a script. It is slower, it costs money per run, it fails in ways a script cannot, and it needs checking a script does not. If the task passes all three, that price buys you something. If not, you paid it for nothing.

show.event: 'Slower and priced per run' slides in

props.sparkLine: It is not a free upgrade.

layers.title: Fails in new ways
layers.sub: confidently, plausibly, and without an error

layers.title: Needs checking a script does not
layers.sub: which is work you now own forever

props.caption: Pass all three and that price buys something. Otherwise you paid it for nothing.

beats.narration_text: And I should be clear that this rubric is a judgement, not a measurement. I chose the three conditions and I scored the six tasks. You may score them differently and that is a useful argument to have. What is not useful is skipping the question because the answer might be no.

props.title: A Judgement, Not a Measurement
props.body: I chose the conditions and scored the tasks. Score them differently and that is a useful argument. Skipping the question because the answer might be no is not.
props.sparkLine: Argue with it. Do not skip it.

beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. Three conditions, all required: the task needs doing rather than describing, a wrong step is cheap to undo, and success is distinguishable from failure without reading every step. Scored against six tasks people genuinely automate, two pass. Each condition fails exactly twice, so there is no single thing to fix. Two out of three is the dangerous score, because an agent that acts and can be undone but cannot be checked will be wrong without anyone noticing. A failed condition is an instruction about what to build instead, and an agent is never a free upgrade over a script. If the task passes all three, the price buys you something.

show.event: the 'two of three' line holds in terracotta

props.artifactHeading: Three conditions, and most tasks fail one
artifactLines: Doing not describing, cheap to undo, checkable without reading every step. All three.
Scored against six commonly automated tasks: two pass.
Each condition fails exactly twice. There is no single villain to fix.
Two of three is the dangerous score — it feels like success while you build it.
A failed condition tells you what to build instead. An agent is never a free upgrade.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Here is a task I want to automate. Score it against three conditions: does it need doing rather than describing, is a wrong step cheap to undo, and can success be told from failure without reading every step. For any condition it fails, tell me what I would have to build first. Then tell me honestly whether a plain script would do. Run it before you start. That last question has saved me more time than any framework.

props.command: Here is a task I want to automate. Score it: does it need doing rather than describing, is a wrong step cheap to undo, can success be told from failure without reading every step? For any condition it fails, what would I have to build first? Then tell me honestly whether a plain script would do.
output: "Would a plain script do?" is the question that saves the most time.
A failed condition is a specification, not a rejection.

beats.narration_text: That was when not to build an agent, and the end of this run through agentic AI. Thanks for watching. Adwait Changan, for Humanitarians AI.
